candidate.answerReason: There are infinitely many distinct backward predecessors of 4, each of which eventually reaches 0 and remains there.

methods.label: Build infinitely many starting values backward
methods.explanation:
Since \(f(4)=0\) and \(f(0)=0\), any starting value that eventually reaches \(4\) produces only finitely many different values. It is enough to construct infinitely many distinct such starting values.

We can work backward because
\[
f(t)=4-(t-2)^2.
\]
For any \(0<a\le4\), one solution of \(f(t)=a\) is
\[
t=2-\sqrt{4-a}.
\]
This root lies in \((0,2]\), so it can serve as another positive starting value.

Define \(a_0=4\) and, for every integer \(k\ge0\), define
\[
a_{k+1}=2-\sqrt{4-a_k}.
\]
The first few values are \(4,2,2-\sqrt2\). By construction, \(f(a_{k+1})=a_k\).

We must check that this process continues indefinitely and gives different numbers. Whenever \(0<a_k\le4\), we have \(0<a_{k+1}\le2\), and
\[
a_k=f(a_{k+1})=a_{k+1}(4-a_{k+1})\ge2a_{k+1}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
0<a_{k+1}\le\frac{a_k}{2}<a_k.
\]
Thus every new term remains in the required range, and the terms are strictly decreasing, hence all distinct.

Starting at \(x_0=a_k\), repeated applications of \(f\) reach \(a_0=4\) after \(k\) steps, then reach \(0\) and stay there. Each constructed starting value therefore has the required property. Since there are infinitely many distinct \(a_k\), the answer is \(\boxed{\text{E, infinitely many}}\).
methods.levelReason: The construction uses elementary recurrences, quadratic equations, square roots, and inequalities. It requires no advanced theory of iteration.

candidate.annotationRationale: The target is to certify infinitely many admissible starting values, including their distinctness. Sequence notation supports the task. The method constructs a backward recurrence by completing the square and taking a square root, then verifies its finite forward behavior. A classification of every possible starting value is unnecessary.

review.mathematicalCheck: The selected root satisfies f(a_{k+1})=a_k and 0<a_{k+1}≤a_k/2<a_k. This proves the construction continues with infinitely many distinct real values. Each reaches 4 and then the fixed value 0, establishing E.
review.levelCheck: The example, root-domain check and distinctness proof make the construction understandable using elementary high-school algebra.
